The three approaches described are sensible and complementary. My substantive recommendation concerns
cadence: it should be event-driven with a calendar floor, not calendar-driven.
Calendar-based reassessment is poorly matched to a technology whose performance changes discontinuously
at the moment of a change rather than continuously with time. I recommend triggering events include, at
minimum: any change to the underlying model version or weights, whether initiated by the manufacturer or
the model provider; any change to system prompts, instructions, or output templates; any change to a retrieval
corpus or knowledge source; any measured shift in the input distribution beyond prespecified bounds; any
change in the deployed sampling configuration; and any accumulation of complaints or adjudicated errors
exceeding a prespecified threshold. A calendar floor — annual, or more frequent for higher-risk devices —
should catch slow drift that trips no discrete trigger.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that postmarket monitoring and reassessment triggers would be maintained as a process separate from the manufacturer's existing design-change procedures, and that such parallel processes tend to diverge over time.
positions.requested_fda_action: Define postmarket monitoring/reassessment triggers as change-control triggers within the manufacturer's quality management system, so the monitoring obligation is integrated with existing design-change procedures rather than run as a separate process.
positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts postmarket monitoring and reassessment triggers but asks FDA to define them as change-control triggers inside the manufacturer's quality management system, integrated with existing design-change procedures, arguing that separate, parallel monitoring processes tend to diverge over time.
positions.source_passage:
From  a  quality-system  perspective  these  should  be  defined  as  change-control  triggers  within  the
manufacturer’s QMS, so that the postmarket monitoring obligation is integrated with existing design-change
procedures rather than maintained as a separate process. Parallel processes diverge.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Human review of every output is not feasible for high-throughput devices, so machine-based supervision is treated as unavoidable; the dominant risk is correlated failure when a supervisory agent is built on the same foundation model as the device, since it shares the same blind spots and its agreement may be misread as independent confirmation.
positions.requested_fda_action: Focus on making automated supervision trustworthy rather than on whether to permit it, including addressing model-family independence between the supervisory agent and the monitored device so that agreement is not credited as independent confirmation.

gap_explanations.deployment_assurance_scalability: The comment frames automated supervision as necessary because human review of every output cannot scale to high-throughput deployment volumes.
gap_explanations.delegated_authority: It raises the reliability of delegating oversight to a machine supervisory agent whose approvals may be mistaken for independent confirmation.

positions.public_summary: Accepts machine-based supervisory agents as unavoidable at high output volumes, shifting the question to trustworthiness rather than permissibility. Warns of correlated failure when the supervisor shares the device's foundation model, since shared blind spots make its agreement look like false independent confirmation.
positions.source_passage:
Automated supervision is probably unavoidable at the volumes involved — human review of every output is
not feasible for a high-throughput device — so the question is how to make it trustworthy rather than whether
to permit it.
... The dominant risk is correlated failure.  A supervisory agent built on the same foundation model as the
device it monitors shares that model’s blind spots. It will approve exactly the outputs that are wrong for
reasons the model family does not represent, and its agreement will be misread as independent confirmation.

positions.stakeholder_concern: A supervisory agent built on the same model family as the device it monitors may share failure modes, and aggregate agreement metrics can mask near-zero sensitivity for serious errors; a monitoring program whose final judgment is machine-made contains no independent check.
positions.requested_fda_action: Accept machine supervisory agents as postmarket evidence only under conditions: require architectural independence (different model family and provider) or reported failure-mode correlation on a held-out error set with evidentiary credit scaled to demonstrated independence; require validation of the supervisor as a measuring instrument via harm-specific sensitivity against human adjudication, re-measured over time; and restrict the supervisor to triage with a human-adjudicated terminal endpoint.

gap_explanations.delegated_authority: The comment argues that terminal adjudication in postmarket monitoring must remain human because a machine-made final judgment leaves no independent check in the loop.
gap_explanations.deployment_assurance_scalability: It frames the supervisory agent's legitimate value as enabling broader sampling of outputs than human reviewers could achieve unaided, while insisting monitoring credit scale with demonstrated supervisor independence and validated sensitivity.

positions.public_summary: Supports machine supervisory agents only for triage, not conclusions. Asks FDA to require supervisors built on a different model family and provider (or reported failure-mode correlation), validation of harm-specific sensitivity against human adjudication with periodic re-measurement, and a human-adjudicated final endpoint.
positions.source_passage:
Architectural  independence  as  a  condition  of  evidentiary  use. A  supervisory  agent  offered  as
postmarket evidence should be built on a model of a different family and provider than the supervised
device. Where full independence is impractical, the sponsor should characterize and report the correlation
in failure modes between supervisor and device on a held-out error set, and the monitoring program’s
credit should scale with the demonstrated independence.
The supervisor is itself a measuring instrument and must be validated as one.  Report its sensitivity
for  the  specific  harms  of  interest  against  human  adjudication  on  a  sampled  basis  —  not  aggregate
agreement, which is dominated by the easy majority of correct outputs and can be high while sensitivity
for serious errors is near zero. Sensitivity must be re-measured over time, since the supervisor’s own
performance drifts.
The supervisor triages; it does not conclude.  Its appropriate role is prioritizing outputs for human
review and enabling broader sampling than humans could achieve unaided. The adjudicated endpoint
should  remain  human.  A  monitoring  program  whose  terminal  judgment  is  machine-made  has  no
independent check anywhere in the loop.

positions.stakeholder_concern: If a machine-based supervisory agent performs postmarket monitoring, modifications to that agent alter the device's monitoring properties, and treating the supervisor as outside the device could leave such changes unassessed.
positions.requested_fda_action: Treat the supervisory agent as part of the device system for change-control purposes, so that changes to the supervisor trigger reassessment on the same terms as changes to the device itself.

gap_explanations.delegated_authority: The comment addresses oversight functions delegated to a machine supervisory agent and argues that the agent's own changes must be governed like device changes because they alter monitoring capability.

positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts use of machine-based supervisory agents for postmarket monitoring but asks FDA to define the supervisor as part of the device system for change control, so modifications to the supervisor trigger the same reassessment as device modifications.
positions.source_passage:
The supervisor is part of the device system  for change-control purposes. A change to the supervisory
agent changes the device’s monitoring properties and should trigger reassessment on the same terms as a
change to the device.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that framing postmarket monitoring as a shared ecosystem could be read as shared responsibility, diluting the manufacturer's complaint-handling, investigation, and reporting duties, even though clinicians, institutions, and societies (and health systems holding outcome data manufacturers lack) are valuable signal sources.
positions.requested_fda_action: State explicitly that signal may come from any source but the duty to investigate and act remains with the manufacturer, and build postmarket roles on existing complaint-handling and MDR architecture rather than a parallel structure.

gap_explanations.distributed_accountability: The comment directly addresses how multi-party postmarket signal sources risk being read as diffusing manufacturer responsibility and asks FDA to anchor accountability explicitly.

positions.public_summary: Supports third-party roles in postmarket monitoring but asks CDRH to state explicitly that manufacturers retain complaint-handling, investigation, and reporting duties regardless of signal source, and to build on existing complaint and MDR structures rather than create a parallel framework.
positions.source_passage:
The accountability principle can be stated simply, and I recommend CDRH state it: information may come
from anywhere; the duty to investigate and act remains with the manufacturer.  Clinicians, institutions,
and societies can be valuable sources of signal, and health systems in particular hold the outcome data
manufacturers lack. But a manufacturer that has arranged to receive signal from third parties has not thereby
delegated any portion of its complaint-handling, investigation, or reporting obligations, and the paper should
say so directly to prevent the shared-ecosystem framing from being read as shared responsibility.
I recommend building on the existing complaint-handling and MDR architecture rather than creating a
parallel  structure.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter states it is currently unclear what constitutes a reportable event or device malfunction for a generative output, using the example of a clinically incorrect recommendation that a clinician recognizes and disregards; under a conventional reading this could imply that hallucinations are reportable malfunctions.
positions.requested_fda_action: Clarify, before postmarket monitoring can function for GenAI-enabled devices, how reportable events and malfunctions are defined for generative outputs, including cases where an incorrect output is caught by the clinician.

gap_explanations.human_ai_system_performance: The comment turns on whether an incorrect generative output intercepted by a clinician counts as a device malfunction, which depends on evaluating the clinician-device system rather than the model alone.

positions.public_summary: While not objecting to postmarket monitoring, the commenter flags an unresolved threshold question: what counts as a reportable event or malfunction for a generative output, including incorrect recommendations a clinician catches and disregards, and asks FDA to clarify before monitoring can operate.
positions.source_passage:
That said, I  want to flag a gap that I believe requires attention before postmarket
monitoring can function at all for these devices:
It is currently unclear what constitutes a reportable event for a generative output. If a device produces a
clinically incorrect recommendation and the clinician recognizes and disregards it, has a device malfunction
occurred? Under a conventional reading, the device did not perform as intended, and a malfunction that could

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that new postmarket performance evaluation mechanisms for GenAI-enabled devices could duplicate existing postmarket infrastructure. They favor leveraging established complaint-handling and medical device reporting (MDR) systems.
positions.requested_fda_action: Build any postmarket monitoring approach for GenAI-enabled devices on the existing complaint-handling and MDR framework rather than establishing a separate, parallel reporting structure.
positions.public_summary: The commenter recommends that FDA's postmarket monitoring approach for GenAI-enabled devices build on existing complaint-handling and medical device reporting systems rather than establishing a parallel structure. The passage does not detail specific monitoring methods or cadence.
positions.source_passage: I recommend building on the existing complaint-handling and MDR architecture rather than creating a parallel  structure.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter states it is unclear what counts as a reportable event or malfunction when a generative output is clinically incorrect but the clinician recognizes and disregards it, and argues this unresolved ambiguity underlies every element of the postmarket section.
positions.requested_fda_action: Asks CDRH to directly define what constitutes a reportable event for generative outputs, and suggests a distinct aggregate reporting channel in which caught errors are reported as rates rather than individual MDRs, to preserve signal without unmanageable event volume.

gap_explanations.human_ai_system_performance: The comment centers on errors that the model produces but the clinician catches, a human-AI interaction outcome that current reporting definitions do not clearly address.
gap_explanations.deployment_assurance_scalability: It raises the practical scalability problem that individual event reporting of caught generative errors would create unmanageable volume, favoring aggregate rate-based reporting.

positions.public_summary: Commenter supports the postmarket section's direction but says it rests on an unresolved question: whether a clinician-caught incorrect generative output is a reportable malfunction. Asks CDRH to define reportable events and consider aggregate, rate-based reporting of caught errors instead of individual MDRs.
positions.source_passage: It is currently unclear what constitutes a reportable event for a generative output. If a device produces a clinically incorrect recommendation and the clinician recognizes and disregards it, has a device malfunction occurred? ... This ambiguity is consequential and unresolved, and every element of Section VI depends on how it is settled. I recommend CDRH address it directly, and would suggest that the workable answer likely involves a distinct, aggregate reporting channel for caught errors — reported as rates rather than as individual MDRs — so that the signal is preserved without generating unmanageable individual-event volume.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that scaling re-evaluation to the apparent magnitude of a modification misses the key question of whether the locked premarket evaluation instrument still validly measures the changed device.
positions.requested_fda_action: Retain the premarket competency assessment as a locked baseline, but categorize post-deployment modifications according to whether the change invalidates the locked benchmark suite rather than by the size of the change.
positions.public_summary: Supports treating the premarket competency assessment as a locked baseline, but proposes that change categorization turn on whether a modification invalidates the locked benchmark suite rather than on the magnitude of the change, since small changes may invalidate evaluation instruments.
positions.source_passage: I support using the premarket competency assessment as a locked baseline. The organizing principle I would propose for categorizing changes is this:  the question is not how large the change is, but whether the locked evaluation instrument remains valid for the changed device.  A small change that invalidates the benchmark suite requires more scrutiny than a large change that does not.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that post-deployment modifications be sorted by their actual potential to affect device outputs, and that a locked benchmark suite remain a valid measuring instrument for whatever change is made. Changes that introduce capabilities the suite does not probe are treated as beyond QMS-managed handling.
positions.requested_fda_action: Adopt a three-tier change framework: Tier 1 (no re-benchmarking) for changes with no path to outputs; Tier 2 (full re-benchmarking against a locked suite within the QMS, no submission) for same-family model version updates, prompt/template changes within a validated structure, validated retrieval corpus refreshes, and sampling changes within a validated range, conditioned on passing at a prespecified non-inferiority margin with inspection-ready documentation; Tier 3 (premarket submission) for change of foundation model family or provider, intended use/user/scope expansion, new input or output modality, changes to agentic tool access or action scope, and any change that invalidates the locked benchmark suite.

gap_explanations.dynamic_intended_use: The proposal ties tier escalation to whether a change introduces capabilities the locked benchmark suite does not probe, framing the validated behavioral envelope rather than only the labeled intended use as the trigger for review.
gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: It distinguishes same-family/same-provider model version updates (QMS-managed with re-benchmarking) from a change of foundation model family or provider (premarket submission), addressing dependence on upstream model suppliers.

positions.public_summary: Proposes three tiers: no re-benchmarking if outputs can't be affected; QMS-managed full re-benchmarking against a locked suite at a prespecified non-inferiority margin for same-family model, prompt, corpus, or sampling changes; premarket submission for model family/provider changes, scope/modality expansion, agentic action changes, or benchmark invalidation.
positions.source_passage:
Tier 1 — no re-benchmarking.  Changes that cannot affect device outputs: user interface presentation, logging, analytics instrumentation, infrastructure changes with no path to the output. Documented under normal change control.
Tier 2 — full re-benchmarking against the locked suite, managed within the QMS, no premarket submission. Model version updates within the same family and provider; prompt or template modifications within  a  validated  structure;  retrieval  corpus  refreshes  drawing  on  a  validated  source  list;  sampling configuration changes within a validated range. The condition is that the device passes the complete locked benchmark  suite  at  a  prespecified  non-inferiority  margin,  with  results  documented  and  available  on inspection. Failure at any element converts the change to Tier 3.
Tier 3 — premarket submission.  Change of foundation model family or provider; expansion of intended use, intended user, or clinical scope; addition of a new input or output modality; any change to agentic tool access or action scope; and any change for which the locked benchmark suite is no longer a valid instrument — for example, a change that introduces capabilities the suite does not probe.

positions.stakeholder_concern: If a sponsor can revise both the device and the benchmark instrument under a lower-tier (Tier 2) change pathway, non-inferiority testing against the revised benchmark becomes meaningless as an assurance of continued performance.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require that the locked benchmark suite cannot be altered under the lower-tier change pathway, and treat any modification of the locked suite as a higher-tier (Tier 3) change requiring the corresponding level of review.
positions.public_summary: Accepts a tiered change-control approach but urges a safeguard: the locked benchmark suite must not be modifiable under the lower tier, since revising device and benchmark together makes non-inferiority meaningless; suite changes should always trigger the highest tier.
positions.source_passage: The essential safeguard is that the benchmark suite itself cannot be modified within Tier 2.  If the sponsor can  revise  the  instrument  and  the  device  together,  non-inferiority  against  the  revised  instrument  is meaningless. Modification of the locked suite should always be a Tier 3 event.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter argues the existing PCCP construct, which prespecifies the specific modification, methods, and impact assessment, does not work for generative devices because the change space is genuinely open — sponsors cannot enumerate future third-party model versions or prompt refinements in advance.
positions.requested_fda_action: Adopt an 'invariant-based' PCCP that locks what must remain true after any change rather than the changes themselves: an escrowed immutable benchmark suite, acceptance thresholds including subgroup thresholds and non-inferiority margin, an independent verification protocol run before changes reach users, rollback criteria and maximum time-to-rollback with technical demonstration, change categories defined by a tier boundary rather than enumeration, and documentation and notification obligations.

gap_explanations.dynamic_intended_use: The proposal defines regulatory control through a fixed behavioral envelope of invariants that must hold after any change, rather than through enumerated modifications, addressing the open-ended evolution of generative device behavior.
gap_explanations.deployment_assurance_scalability: It centers assurance on pre-release verification, independence in who runs it, and demonstrated rollback capability with a maximum time-to-rollback before changes reach users.

positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts change-control adaptation but says prespecifying modifications fails for generative devices with open change spaces. Proposes an 'invariant-based' PCCP locking escrowed benchmarks, subgroup acceptance thresholds and non-inferiority margins, independent pre-release verification, demonstrated rollback with time limits, tier-defined change categories, and notification duties.
positions.source_passage:
The current PCCP construct prespecifies what will change  — the modification, the methods to implement and validate it, the impact assessment. For generative devices this fails, not because sponsors are unwilling but because the change space is genuinely open: a sponsor cannot enumerate in advance the model versions a provider will release or the prompt refinements that experience will suggest.
The adaptation is to invert what is locked. An invariant-based PCCP prespecifies not the change but what must remain true after any change:
The evaluation instrument — the complete benchmark suite, escrowed and immutable.
The acceptance thresholds, including subgroup-level thresholds and the non-inferiority margin.
The verification protocol — what is run, in what order, by whom, with what independence, before any change reaches users.
The  rollback  criteria  and  mechanism,  including  maximum  time-to-rollback  and  the  technical demonstration that rollback is achievable.
The  change categories in scope , defined by the Tier 2 boundary above rather than by enumeration of specific changes.
The documentation and notification obligations attaching to each change.

positions.stakeholder_concern: If a sponsor can alter its benchmark suite at the same time it alters the device, the change-control construct becomes circular and yields no real assurance of continued safety or effectiveness.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require that the benchmark suite be locked and escrowed, and that any change to the suite itself be treated at the highest review tier (Tier 3) rather than managed at the sponsor's discretion.

gap_explanations.delegated_authority: The comment warns that leaving control of the evaluation instrument in sponsor hands undermines the assurance value of any delegated change-control mechanism, so modifications to the benchmark itself must remain subject to FDA review.

positions.public_summary: Supports the change-control construct only if the benchmark suite is locked and escrowed, with any modification to the suite subject to the highest-tier review. Warns that sponsor-modifiable benchmarks make evaluation circular and provide no assurance, treating these safeguards as essential rather than optional.
positions.source_passage: The construct depends entirely on the integrity of the locked instrument. If the sponsor can modify the benchmark suite while modifying the device, the whole thing is circular and provides no assurance at all. Escrow of the suite, and Tier 3 treatment of any change to it, are not optional features of this proposal — they are the proposal.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Devices built on third-party foundation models may be exposed to provider-initiated model changes if the manufacturer cannot lock to a specific model version; the commenter treats the absence of version pinning and change notice as a design deficiency rather than an acceptable residual risk.
positions.requested_fda_action: CDRH should explicitly state that GenAI-enabled devices relying on third-party models are expected to execute against a pinned, version-identified model endpoint, and that inability to pin (or use of a provider lacking pinning with change notice) must be remediated as a design control matter.

gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: The comment makes the foundation model provider's technical offerings—version pinning and change notification—a precondition for device design adequacy, framing supplier capability as a quality requirement rather than a manufacturer-managed risk.
gap_explanations.distributed_accountability: It addresses how responsibility for provider-initiated model changes should be allocated by requiring the device manufacturer to control the model version it executes against.

positions.public_summary: Endorses addressing third-party model changes but asks CDRH to go further: state that GenAI devices must run against a pinned, version-identified model endpoint, and that inability to pin, or use of providers without pinning and change notice, is a design deficiency requiring correction.
positions.source_passage: Treat version pinning as a design control expectation.  CDRH should state that a GenAI-enabled device relying on a third-party model is expected to execute against a pinned, version-identified model endpoint, and that the inability to pin — or reliance on a provider that does not offer pinning with change notice — is a design deficiency to be addressed, not a residual risk to be accepted. This is the single highest-leverage statement CDRH could make in this area, and it would immediately reshape provider offerings in the medical device segment.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Device manufacturers relying on third-party foundation models may not have enough advance warning of developer-initiated model changes to complete re-evaluation before the change takes effect, and pinned model versions may be retired too quickly.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require contractual advance-notice provisions with a defined minimum notice period long enough to complete the referenced Tier 2 re-benchmarking before a change takes effect, plus a minimum deprecation window for pinned model versions.

gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: The comment seeks enforceable supplier-side obligations—minimum change-notice periods and version deprecation windows—so that upstream foundation model developers' actions do not outpace the device manufacturer's ability to re-validate.

positions.public_summary: Supports contractual mechanisms for third-party model changes but asks FDA to require defined minimums: an advance change-notice period long enough to complete Tier 2 re-benchmarking before a change takes effect, and a minimum deprecation window for pinned model versions.
positions.source_passage: Require contractual change notice with a defined minimum period , sufficient to complete the Tier 2 re-benchmarking described above before a change takes effect, together with a minimum deprecation window for pinned versions.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Contractual commitments from third-party hosted model providers cannot be verified in real time, so silent upstream model changes may go undetected in deployed devices.
positions.requested_fda_action: CDRH should describe continuous 'canary' monitoring — a small fixed probe suite of inputs with known expected outputs run frequently against the live endpoint — as an expected element of postmarket monitoring for any device built on a third-party hosted model.

gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: The comment argues contractual mechanisms with third-party model suppliers are unverifiable in real time and must be replaced by direct technical verification of endpoint stability.
gap_explanations.deployment_assurance_scalability: It proposes continuous automated probing of the live deployed endpoint as a low-cost way to detect silent change, rather than relying on periodic or assumption-based assurance.

positions.public_summary: Supports postmarket monitoring of third-party model dependencies but asks FDA to go further: because supplier contracts cannot be verified in real time, CDRH should treat continuous high-frequency 'canary' probe testing against live endpoints as an expected monitoring element for hosted-model devices.
positions.source_passage: Require continuous canary monitoring, because contracts cannot be verified in real time.  A small, fixed probe suite — a set of inputs with known expected outputs — executed against the live endpoint at high frequency  provides  direct  detection  of  silent  upstream  change.  This  is  inexpensive,  technically straightforward, and the only mechanism I am aware of that verifies rather than assumes endpoint stability. I recommend CDRH describe it as an expected element of postmarket monitoring for any device on a third-party hosted model.

positions.stakeholder_concern: When a foundation model provider deprecates a pinned version, the manufacturer's forced migration produces a device running on a materially different model; the commenter is concerned that the involuntary nature of the change could be used to justify reduced re-evaluation.
positions.requested_fda_action: Classify provider-forced model migrations as a Tier 3 (highest-scrutiny) change and explicitly foreclose lighter treatment because the migration was involuntary, while expecting manufacturers to address the contingency in design planning, including maintaining a validated fallback.

gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: The position centers on upstream foundation model providers deprecating pinned versions, requiring manufacturers to pre-plan validated fallbacks as a supplier-dependency control.
gap_explanations.distributed_accountability: The commenter argues that a change initiated by a third-party provider does not dilute the manufacturer's obligation to re-evaluate the resulting device.

positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts a tiered change-control approach but asks FDA to classify provider-forced foundation model migrations as the highest tier, explicitly rejecting lighter treatment because the change was involuntary, and to expect manufacturers to plan ahead with a validated fallback version.
positions.source_passage: Treat provider-forced migration as a Tier 3 change. When a provider deprecates a pinned version and the manufacturer must migrate, the resulting device is running on a different model. That it was involuntary does not change what it is, and the paper should foreclose the argument that forced migrations warrant lighter treatment.  Manufacturers  should  be  expected  to  plan  for  this  contingency  —  including  maintaining  a validated fallback — as part of design planning rather than handling it as an emergency.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Manufacturers and CDRH currently have to infer dependency risk from third-party foundation model behavior rather than assess it directly, because model versioning, deprecation, and change-notification practices are not documented in any standing record.
positions.requested_fda_action: Advance the Foundation Model Master File concept as a maintained, current record covering model versioning, deprecation, and change-notification practices so dependency risk can be assessed directly.

gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: The comment frames the MAF as a mechanism for documenting an upstream model supplier's versioning, deprecation, and change-notification practices so downstream dependency risk can be evaluated.

positions.public_summary: Supports the voluntary Foundation Model Master File concept, stating it would be most valuable as a standing, current record of a model's versioning, deprecation, and change-notification practices, enabling FDA and manufacturers to assess dependency risk directly rather than by inference.
positions.source_passage: I would also note that this is where a Foundation Model MAF (Question 25) would deliver the most value: a standing, current record of a model's versioning, deprecation, and change-notification practices would let CDRH and manufacturers assess dependency risk directly rather than by inference.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter agrees with CDRH's assessment that foundation model developers have little incentive to voluntarily disclose safety-relevant limitations, since medical devices are a small revenue share and disclosure carries competitive and litigation exposure, so a purely voluntary MAF program is unlikely to attract broad participation on its own.
positions.requested_fda_action: Create the voluntary Foundation Model MAF program but pair it with a manufacturer-side default: where no MAF exists, the device manufacturer must independently generate and fund full model characterization (training data provenance as determinable, contamination assessment, known failure modes, version and deprecation practices, subgroup performance) or the submission is incomplete, thereby creating a procurement preference for models with MAFs.

gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: The comment proposes using submission-completeness requirements to pressure upstream foundation model suppliers into documenting provenance, failure modes, versioning, and deprecation practices that device manufacturers cannot otherwise obtain.
gap_explanations.evidence_burden_commercial_viability: The proposal deliberately places the full cost of independent model characterization on the device manufacturer when no MAF exists, shifting evidence burden as a lever on supplier behavior.

positions.public_summary: Agrees with FDA that voluntary Foundation Model MAFs face weak developer incentives, but recommends creating the program anyway and adding a manufacturer-side default: absent an MAF, the manufacturer must independently fund full model characterization or the submission is incomplete, creating procurement pressure.
positions.source_passage:
The paper's candor about the incentive problem is warranted. Foundation model developers serve markets in which  medical  devices  are  a  small  fraction  of  revenue;  disclosure  of  safety-relevant  limitations  carries competitive and litigation exposure; and a voluntary program asking them to document weaknesses for a regulator overseeing someone else's product is unlikely to attract broad participation on its own merits.
I nonetheless recommend CDRH create it, because the mechanism that makes it work is not the model developer's incentive — it is the device manufacturer's.
Pair  the  voluntary  MAF  with  a  manufacturer-side  default:  where  an  MAF  is  absent,  the  device manufacturer bears the full characterization burden for the underlying model. Training data provenance to  the  extent  determinable,  contamination  assessment,  known  failure  modes,  version  and  deprecation practices, subgroup performance characterization — all of it, generated independently at the manufacturer's cost, or the submission is incomplete.
That default creates a procurement preference.

positions.stakeholder_concern: A Foundation Model MAF is only useful if it contains specific safety-relevant content (version lineage, training data cutoff, change/deprecation policy, known failure modes, refusal behavior, developer evaluations, medical fine-tuning) and is kept current; a one-time snapshot would not support contamination analysis or detection of developer-initiated model changes.
positions.requested_fda_action: Specify the enumerated MAF content elements and impose a currency requirement obligating updates within a defined period after any model change.

gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: The comment focuses on what upstream foundation model developers must disclose and maintain—version lineage, change notification, deprecation policy, and documented failure modes—as a precondition for device-level assurance.

positions.public_summary: Accepts the voluntary Foundation Model MAF concept but asks FDA to specify content—model identity and version lineage, training data cutoff, change/deprecation policy, known failure modes, refusal behavior, developer evaluations, medical fine-tuning—and to require updates within a defined period after any model change.
positions.source_passage: Suggested MAF content: model identity and version lineage; training data cutoff date (essential for the contamination analysis under Question 10); versioning, change notification, and deprecation policy (essential for Question 24); known limitations and documented failure modes; safety training and refusal behavior; evaluation results the developer has generated; and any medical-domain-specific training or fine-tuning. A currency requirement — the MAF must be updated within a defined period of any model change — is what makes it useful rather than a snapshot.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that a Foundation Model MAF could be misread as evidence of the safety or effectiveness of devices built on that model, displacing evaluation of the finished device.
positions.requested_fda_action: Explicitly frame the MAF as contextual information supporting, not substituting for, evaluation of the final user-facing device as configured for deployment, consistent with the paper's statement on the unit of evaluation.

gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: The comment addresses how upstream foundation model documentation should be weighted relative to device-level evidence, cautioning that supplier-provided information cannot carry assurance for the downstream device.

positions.public_summary: Accepts the Foundation Model MAF concept but cautions it should never be treated as establishing a downstream device's safety or effectiveness. Endorses FDA's statement that the final user-facing device as deployed is the unit of evaluation, with MAFs serving only as context.
positions.source_passage: I would add one caution: an MAF should never be treated as establishing the safety or effectiveness of any device built on the model. The paper's statement that the unit of evaluation is the final user-facing device as configured for deployment is correct and important, and the MAF should be framed as context for that evaluation, not as a partial substitute for it.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Per-step accuracy metrics overstate end-to-end reliability for multi-step agentic devices, since compounding error across a sequence (e.g., 95% per step over ten steps yields roughly 60% task success) means step-level results do not reflect whether the completed task is performed correctly.
positions.requested_fda_action: CDRH should explicitly state that acceptance criteria and evaluation for agentic GenAI-enabled devices must be defined and measured at the level of completed task/trajectory rather than individual step accuracy, anticipating that sponsors will otherwise submit easier-to-generate step-level metrics.
positions.public_summary: Commenter agrees agentic devices need distinct oversight but asks CDRH to state explicitly that acceptance criteria and evaluation be set at the completed-task (trajectory) level, not per-step accuracy, because compounding step errors make step-level metrics misleading for multi-step tasks.
positions.source_passage: Trajectory-level  acceptance  criteria. Per-step  performance  is  a  misleading  summary  of  end-to-end reliability. A device that completes each step correctly 95% of the time completes a ten-step task correctly about 60% of the time, and that arithmetic is unforgiving as sequences lengthen. Acceptance criteria must be stated at the level of the completed task, and evaluation must measure task completion rather than step accuracy. I recommend CDRH state this explicitly, because step-level metrics are far easier to generate and will otherwise be offered.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Agentic systems can take actions—tool calls, write operations, effects on external systems—whose consequences vary in reversibility, and unbounded or silently expanded action capability is not adequately controlled by existing framing.
positions.requested_fda_action: Require sponsors to submit an enumerated inventory of every action the system can take, each classified by reversibility and consequence of erroneous execution, require explicit qualified-user confirmation for irreversible actions, and treat the inventory as a locked specification whose expansion is a Tier 3 change.

gap_explanations.dynamic_intended_use: Treating the enumerated action inventory as a locked specification defines a behavioral envelope whose expansion triggers heightened review, going beyond a static intended-use statement.
gap_explanations.delegated_authority: The recommendation limits how much authority an agent may exercise autonomously by requiring explicit qualified-user confirmation before irreversible actions.
gap_explanations.operational_harm: The inventory covers write operations and effects on external systems, framing harm in terms of erroneous execution against downstream systems rather than only incorrect clinical output.

positions.public_summary: Recommends that FDA require agentic device sponsors to submit an enumerated inventory of every possible action—tools, write operations, external systems affected—classified by reversibility and consequence of erroneous execution, with explicit user confirmation for irreversible actions and inventory expansion treated as a Tier 3 change.
positions.source_passage: Action inventory with irreversibility classification. I recommend sponsors submit an enumerated inventory of every action the system can take — every tool, every write operation, every external system it can affect — each classified by reversibility and by the consequence of erroneous execution. Irreversible actions should require explicit confirmation by a qualified user, and the inventory should be treated as a locked specification whose expansion is a Tier 3 change under the framework in Question 22.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Agentic GenAI devices could hold broader tool permissions than their intended use requires, and the discussion paper risks creating a separate treatment that duplicates CDRH's existing cybersecurity expectations.
positions.requested_fda_action: Expect agentic systems to operate under least-privilege tool access scoped per deployment, and cross-reference CDRH's existing cybersecurity expectations rather than developing a parallel framework.

gap_explanations.cybersecurity_as_safety: The comment ties agentic device safety directly to established security practice and CDRH cybersecurity expectations rather than treating them as separate domains.
gap_explanations.delegated_authority: It addresses how much authority an agentic system should be granted, recommending permissions be limited to the narrowest scope sufficient for the intended use in each deployment.

positions.public_summary: Supports addressing agentic systems but recommends FDA specify least-privilege tool access, with permissions scoped per deployment to the narrowest set sufficient for the intended use, and cross-reference existing CDRH cybersecurity expectations instead of creating a parallel treatment.
positions.source_passage: Least-privilege  tool  access. Agentic  systems  should  hold  the  narrowest  permissions  sufficient  for  the intended use, scoped per deployment. This is standard security practice and maps directly onto CDRH's existing cybersecurity expectations; I recommend the paper cross-reference them rather than developing a parallel treatment.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Without audit logs capable of reconstructing the full agentic trajectory — inputs, intermediate reasoning artifacts, tool calls, returned values, actions taken, and the model version and configuration in effect — root cause analysis of harmful outcomes is impossible and corrective action becomes guesswork, and complaint-handling obligations discussed under Question 21 cannot be met.
positions.requested_fda_action: Make the adequacy of audit logging an explicit element of premarket review for agentic GenAI-enabled devices, rather than assuming it will be addressed postmarket.

gap_explanations.distributed_accountability: The comment ties traceability of agentic behavior directly to the ability of manufacturers and others to discharge complaint-handling and corrective-action responsibilities after a harmful outcome.
gap_explanations.delegated_authority: It focuses on reconstructing autonomous multi-step actions such as tool calls and executed actions, an oversight need arising specifically from authority delegated to the agent.

positions.public_summary: Commenter supports attention to agentic device oversight but asks FDA to make audit logging adequacy an explicit premarket review element rather than a postmarket assumption, arguing full trajectory reconstruction — inputs, tool calls, actions, model version — is necessary for root cause analysis and complaint
positions.source_passage: Audit logging sufficient for post-hoc reconstruction. When an agentic system produces a harmful outcome, the investigation must be able to reconstruct the full trajectory — inputs, intermediate reasoning artifacts where available, tool calls, returned values, actions taken, and the model version and configuration in effect. Without this, root cause analysis is not possible, corrective action is guesswork, and the complaint-handling obligations under Question 21 cannot be discharged. I recommend audit logging adequacy be an explicit premarket review element for agentic devices rather than a postmarket assumption.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter argues that agentic devices are precisely where end-to-end performance is hardest to establish before market entry while compounding errors propagate fastest and are least reversible after deployment, making them a poor fit for trading premarket evidence for postmarket monitoring.
positions.requested_fda_action: CDRH should treat agentic GenAI-enabled devices as presumptively ineligible for the reduced-premarket-evidence pathway contemplated in Question 18.

gap_explanations.operational_harm: The comment emphasizes that errors in agentic devices propagate rapidly and are least reversible once deployed, a harm dynamic not fully captured by the premarket/postmarket evidence trade-off as framed.
gap_explanations.delegated_authority: The concern arises from autonomous multi-step agentic action where compounding errors occur with limited human interruption, making delegated decision authority the source of the elevated risk.

positions.public_summary: Commenter warns that the proposed trade of premarket evidence for postmarket monitoring fits agentic devices poorly, since end-to-end performance is hardest to establish premarket while errors compound fastest and are least reversible. Recommends CDRH presumptively exclude agentic devices from that pathway.
positions.source_passage: I would also note that the compounding-error arithmetic above interacts badly with the premarket-uncertainty trade proposed in Question 18. Agentic devices are where end-to-end performance is hardest to establish premarket,  and  simultaneously  where  errors  propagate  fastest  and  are  least  reversible  postmarket.  I recommend CDRH treat agentic devices as presumptively outside the reduced-premarket-evidence pathway.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that without an explicit, published mapping from risk tier to required evidence, the framework will lack predictability, and that a 'competency-based' approach may not in practice be the 'least burdensome' one.
positions.requested_fda_action: Publish the risk-tier-to-evidence mapping so sponsors can predict the level of evidence expected for a given risk tier.

gap_explanations.evidence_burden_commercial_viability: The comment ties predictability of evidence expectations directly to regulatory burden, arguing that an unpublished mapping risks making the competency-based approach more burdensome than intended.

positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts pairing the risk framework with the competency-based approach but asks FDA to publish an explicit risk-tier-to-evidence mapping, arguing that predictability is what makes risk-based frameworks less burdensome and that otherwise "competency-based" and "least burdensome" may diverge.
positions.source_passage: Publish  the  risk-tier-to-evidence  mapping. Predictability  is  the  mechanism  by  which  risk-based frameworks reduce burden. Without it, "competency-based" and "least burdensome" will not describe the same thing.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that the proposed framework could create documentation and assessment artifacts that run parallel to, rather than build on, manufacturers' existing ISO 14971 risk files, design controls, and QMSR change control procedures.
positions.requested_fda_action: FDA should ground the competency-based framework and modification re-evaluation in existing quality system and risk management infrastructure instead of creating separate artifacts, and should explain in the paper how the new framework elements relate to those existing requirements.
positions.public_summary: Accepts the framework's general direction but asks FDA to build on existing ISO 14971 risk files, design controls, and QMSR change control rather than creating parallel artifacts, and to explain explicitly how the new framework elements relate to those existing requirements.
positions.source_passage: Integrate with existing quality system and risk management infrastructure.  Manufacturers maintain ISO 14971 risk files, design controls, and change control procedures under the QMSR. The framework should draw on these rather than establishing parallel artifacts, and the paper should state how the pieces relate.

positions.stakeholder_concern: Several elements of the framework — enforceable postmarket conditions with automatic consequences, third-party recognition regimes, and obligations reaching foundation model developers who are not device manufacturers — appear to sit at or beyond the limits of existing statutory authority, and the paper defers the question.
positions.requested_fda_action: CDRH should revisit and explicitly identify which proposed elements it can implement under current authorities and which would require new legislation, so stakeholders know which parts of the framework to build toward.

gap_explanations.delegated_authority: The comment flags third-party recognition regimes as potentially exceeding existing FDA authority, raising the question of the legal basis for delegating assessment functions.
gap_explanations.distributed_accountability: It questions FDA's authority to impose obligations on foundation model developers who are not device manufacturers, a distributed-responsibility issue the paper leaves unresolved.

positions.public_summary: Commenter accepts the framework's direction but urges CDRH to stop deferring the legal-authority question, noting that enforceable postmarket conditions, third-party recognition, and obligations on non-manufacturer foundation model developers may exceed current authorities and could require congressional action.
positions.source_passage: Identify  which  elements  require  new  legal  authority. The  paper  expressly  defers  this  question.  I understand why, but I would encourage CDRH to return to it, because several proposals — enforceable postmarket conditions with automatic consequences, third-party recognition regimes, obligations touching foundation model developers who are not device manufacturers — appear to sit at or beyond the edge of existing authorities. Stakeholders assessing which parts of this framework to build toward would benefit from knowing which parts CDRH can implement and which would require Congress.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter observes that the discussion paper is framed toward enabling market entry and worries the competency-based approach could be read as an authorization pathway rather than a genuine evaluation framework.
positions.requested_fda_action: State explicitly that the competency-based framework contemplates the outcome that a given intended use is not currently supportable by available evidence, so it is understood as an evaluation framework rather than an authorization pathway.
positions.public_summary: Accepts the competency-based framework but asks CDRH to state explicitly that it can conclude an intended use is not currently supportable by available evidence, so the approach is understood as an evaluation framework rather than an authorization pathway.
positions.source_passage: Preserve  the  option  to  say  no. The  paper's  framing  is  oriented  toward  enabling  market  entry, appropriately  so  given  its  purpose.  But  a  competency-based  framework  should  also  be  capable  of concluding  that  a  given  intended  use  is  not  currently  supportable  by  available  evidence.  I  would encourage CDRH to state that the framework contemplates that outcome, so that it is understood as an evaluation framework rather than an authorization pathway.

positions.stakeholder_concern: The commenter is concerned that the framework's flexibility exceeds the supporting infrastructure: benchmarks that are not yet trustworthy, unsettled postmarket reportability rules, third-party foundation model dependencies manufacturers cannot control, and a nonexistent third-party assessment capacity.
positions.requested_fda_action: Sequence implementation so that the enabling infrastructure (trustworthy benchmarks, clear reportability rules, mechanisms for third-party model change control, and qualified third-party assessment capacity) is established before the flexible evidentiary pathways are relied upon.

gap_explanations.deployment_assurance_scalability: The comment states that third-party assessment capacity and benchmark trustworthiness do not yet exist at the scale the framework assumes, making the flexible approach unworkable in practice until that infrastructure is built.
gap_explanations.ai_supplier_quality: The comment identifies third-party foundation model dependencies as something manufacturers cannot presently control, a supplier-control problem the questions treat as manageable by the manufacturer.

positions.public_summary: Accepts the framework's general direction but argues its flexibility currently exceeds supporting infrastructure — untrustworthy benchmarks, unsettled postmarket reportability rules, uncontrollable third-party model dependencies, and absent third-party assessment capacity. Asks FDA to build that infrastructure before relying on flexible evidentiary pathways.
positions.source_passage: My central concern is that the framework's flexibility currently outruns the infrastructure needed to make flexibility safe: benchmarks that cannot yet be trusted, postmarket monitoring whose reportability rules are unsettled,  third-party  model  dependencies  that  manufacturers  cannot  presently  control,  and  third-party assessment capacity that does not yet exist. Each of these is addressable, and several are addressable now. But the flexibility and the infrastructure should arrive in that order — infrastructure first — rather than the reverse.
